utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I noticed that there was no number given to the exhibit yesterday. I'd like a number to be given, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What is the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be 374, Prosecutor's Exhibit. That will be the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we prepared an application for the appeal for one of the decisions of the Trial Chamber, and I would like to tender it to the Registrar at this point for your review and consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It should not be given to us. If it is an appeal, you should file it with the Registrar, with the Registrar or the Registry. Then it probably will go to, I assume, depending on the applicable Rule, it will go to a panel of three Judges who will decide whether or not to grant leave to appeal. Thank you. All right. So we continue with the cross-examination by Counsel Pasaric. Counsel Pasaric, before you start, may I ask you to be so kind as to put your questions clearly and succinctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Bringa. Good morning, Your Honours. I have really made an effort to reduce my questions, and I also received a transcript of the videotape yesterday. I thank the Registry for it, and I prepared some questions which I believe can be answered very clearly and shortly, but I would just like to stay with the general remarks. This is where we left off yesterday. We talked about the situation in which both the Muslims and the Croats were allies against the Serbs at the beginning the war. Could you tell me, and you refer to your book, during World War II the Croatian government, which worked with the axis powers, was persecuting Serbs, but you do not mention anything else. Does that mean -- did you imply that the Croats and Muslims did not have any conflict during World War II?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'll talk about the area that I know the best, which is the Central Bosnia. To my knowledge, there was no fighting between Croats and Muslims in that area except when Muslims or Croats found themselves on --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I have no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I take it there's no translation into Serbo-Croat. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: They have changed the channel. All right. Professor Bringa, you may continue. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Today I'll only talk about the area which I know the best, which is Central Bosnia. To my knowledge, there were no clashes between -- no, Muslims and Croats or Bosniaks and Croats did not find themselves on different sides in the Second World War except when Muslims were soldiers in the -- or sided with the partisans, and Croats on the opposite sided with -- and vice versa, I guess. There were Croats also who fought with the partisans. So I know in this particular village, there didn't come -- there was fighting up further in the hills but there was no actual clashes. There were no clashes in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: My question refers to a witness who explained his involvement. He's siding with the HVO, based on the fact that his father had sided with the Croats during World War II. So there were some alliances between the two parties during World War II; right?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. As I stated, there were individuals who were siding -- there were Muslims who were siding with the so-called Croatian independent state during the Second World War. There were also Muslims who were with the partisans. There were Croats with the partisans. So it's quite a complex picture. I am aware that there were Bosniaks who were mobilised in the HVO, particularly in the beginning the war, because that was the army that was the most organised. This was particularly the case in the Mostar area and Sarajevo, the cities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Perhaps this is not a question, because I think that there was no reason for the Croats and Muslims to be allies until the very end in this war.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Is this a question? In which case, I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Yes. So what I'm saying is it is not a question, because this could have been expected. I think it just flows logically. So perhaps let's move on. Yesterday we mentioned a referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which took place on 3 March, 1992. Do you know what was the issue? What was the question on that referendum, because perhaps yesterday it was left slightly unclear?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you put this question in a context, because I'm not quite -- I don't quite understand what the point is of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I asked whether in this referendum the Muslims and the Croats voted together for the question which was asked at the referendum. So what was exactly the question which was to be answered in this referendum?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't have either the statistics in front of me of how many Croats and how many Bosniaks voted but, yes, as I understand it, there were Croats who voted for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Of course there were, yes. The math is there. Otherwise, the Bosniaks themselves could not have done it. I know that you do not have the exact figures, but you could assume that they must have since the referendum passed, but can you tell us what was the referendum deciding on?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: ... on what people were telling me what they vote. For them -- the choice that represented for them was to whether to stay in a Yugoslavia, which by then would be dominated by Serbs and where they would feel -- dominated by Serbs and also a not very democratic Serbia, or whether they would want independence. This is how they presented the choice to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: If I told you that the question was for the sovereign and whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: So that is how it was; right?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question referring to what we were talking yesterday, were there any ethnic differences way before this war? On page 111 in your book, you mention that the Muslims and Croats, the young ones, had separate dances, that they were going dancing, doesn't matter where, but they went to separate places, and that the youth organisation, which was an official organisation, organised them separately for Muslims on the one day and for Croats on another day, and that until the '70s, the young Croats and Muslims were not allowed to talk to each other, to intermingle, which surprised me quite a bit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was a tradition whereby young Croats would go to the dances on Fridays, which is a holy day for the Muslims, and they would go on Saturday. Now, this was -- again, I'm talking in my book about the undesirability of mixed marriages, and I assumed it had to do this fact, because at the dances, of course, young people are flirting. That's where they find their partner. That's where they find the person they'll marry in this rural community. It used to be like that. Of course, more recently you have coffee bars, you have cafeterias, places where they mix. There wasn't that -- there was also this traditional thing going on, but it was on the decline and it was increasingly popular to go into the more urban centres and go to modern coffee bars where they would all meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: So things were developing for better, but until the '70s they were not allowed to talk to each other?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Okay. Of course they were allowed to talk to each other. This is the way it was put by a young woman who told me how it was for her sister. I don't think it was -- some parents would say, you know, that you should not -- this had to do with young people, about going out with young people, and they should not talk to one of the opposite sex from the opposite group, and again, that had to do with the undesirability of mixed marriages, which I talk about quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: What you wrote down in your book is what you heard in a Muslim family?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I got it from both sides. I also heard it from young Croat women. But it doesn't mean that everybody followed that. Like so many prohibitions when you're young, it doesn't mean that everybody followed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this is a serious indication about what was going on in that area at the time. Also, yesterday you said something about the complex causes of this conflict, and I pointed out that I was surprised by the mention in your book of the Vance-Owen Plan and its catastrophic consequences in Central Bosnia, and in the film, this plan is also mentioned. Why do you think that this plan, Vance-Owen Plan, had catastrophic consequences in the area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, firstly because these provinces were ethnically defined and political representation was ethnically defined, and this would feed into the current situation whereby, again, political representation was ethnic, and I think -- my view is that it would undermine what they were trying to preserve, a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina. Already there were political aims, there were political attempts, and later also military, in trying to carve out a Croatian state after Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the wake, I think, of the Serbian attempt, and this is no secret, that there was from Zagreb a desire to carve out a Croatian state in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, as soon as you had a peace plan which assigned an area of Bosnia-Herzegovina which then was called Croatian, this was seen, in my mind, as a go-ahead for the Croatian authorities in the Croatian-controlled areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina to also -- which they may have felt was then legitimate in some ways, to grab that territory. Now, this is -- some of these areas were, of course, mixed, and the problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina with defining an area, a geographical area, as ethnic, was the idea which I think originated from a lack of democratic political pluralist tradition whereby when you are in control, again when it is defined as the area of one group and when your group is in control, it means total control in the way that there used to be a one-party system, Communist Party, which had total control. This was then transferred to the idea that if it is Croatian or Serbian or whatever, that would be total control by that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: This is the consequence of fact, that this, as people called them, were the first democratic elections, so the democratic traditions did not go back for hundreds of years. But as the party had been divided along certain lines, be it ethnic or economic, so I assume that the parties which won those elections had legitimacy in assuming power and control over these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pasaric, sorry to interrupt you, but instead of commenting on the answers of the witness or expressing your views, why don't you ask questions? This is the purpose of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was trying to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: My question is: This was to be expected, since they won in the elections; isn't this so?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry? What was to be expected?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: That the authorities in certain local constituencies would be assumed by those who won, and since the other parties were divided or broken down along ethnic lines, I assume that it was to be expected that they would organise, that they would assume power there where they had won.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, for someone who comes from a democratic tradition, I do not think that it was expected that that implied excluding the other group completely and expelling them from the areas that they controlled and burning down their villages and houses. I do not think that was to be expected. It should not have been happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Of course not, and I do not believe that this is what went on in the beginning. My question -- the question which I'm posing to you: In the area which concerns us, this is how the authority was set up and the minority party then split off, and I apologise for this clarification. I think that it was just part of a budding democratic tradition. When we talked about the Vance-Owen Plan, which was mentioned by several people in the film, does that mean that people, when they were proposed something by the International Community, that they were more likely to accept it than when it was proposed on the local level? Let's say, if they said, "We should break down the country into cantons," and this came from the International Community, that it sort of carried more weight than had it been proposed at the local level within Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, as transpires in the film, the people were not very keen on this plan. They had hoped they would be in so-called neutral Sarajevo, which would mean that they could continue the kind of life that they associated with living in Bosnia, which was multi-ethnic and multi-cultural, because if it was neutral Sarajevo, it would not be ethnically defined. What they were worried about was to end up in a province, a canton, which was completely run by Croats. The other point about, were they more willing to accept it, well, the international peace plans, they were reached through negotiations. The alternative which we ended up with was reached through military action and through a lot of suffering, and that is the difference. One was obtained by military force and the other one was then negotiated over the negotiating table by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: So they may have had more confidence. And if I understood you correctly, you mentioned that the children were being sent to the areas which were earmarked to become Muslim.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand the point of your question but, yes, they did send their children away to an area -- as I said yesterday, what they worried the most about was not shells and bombs, which there were plenty of in the Visoko area, what they were worried about was the people, the foot soldiers, who would come into their house and break into their houses and attack them in a very personal way and commit atrocities in front of, sometimes their children and sometimes in front of other family members and attack their very being, their very -- you know, the sense of their identity, by going in and attacking them personally. It was a very personalised violence, which was what they were terrified of, because that was what would break down their identity, the core of their identity, and that's what they were worried about, not the shells and the bombs. So they would send their children over to, yes, this area, which was under intense bombing and shelling, but at least, because it was controlled at the time by the Bosnian army, they knew that there wouldn't be people who would enter their homes, they hoped at least; they felt more safe there. While in the area where we're talking about, they had seen that the danger was moving closer and closer and they had heard stories about what was happening and they were terrified about what was going to happen if they entered that particular village. This is also expressed in the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: I must say that I did not find it in the film. They just said there that the child was being sent to the area controlled by the Muslims, so I question your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry. I was trying to explain to you why they felt that was a safe area in spite of it being shelled, in spite of it being under attack now from the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. You mentioned that when you were first there, that there was joint guards, and then they had split up while you were there. There were also several further indications that while you were there the first time around, which was in February, late February 1993, something took place --

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... late January and the first two weeks of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Right. Do you know what actually took place there at that time? Not in the village itself but what caused these joint guards to split up?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The only explanation I was given was that the Croatian members of the common guard were locals from the village, had received an order from HVO command, I don't know, in Kiseljak, that they should discontinue these common patrols, and I cannot say the reason for that. That, you would have to ask the people who gave the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Tell us, at that time, you did not hear about any atrocities or massacres? The name of Dusina doesn't mean a thing to you?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dusina? No. I know Dusina, I've been to Dusina, but -- and I was there in '93, but this is -- and I know it from coverage of this case, but I did not hear about that neither from the Croats nor from the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Also, Josefina, Slavka's sister, I think, had fled. That is also mentioned. She went about 10 miles away, that is to say, 15 kilometres away, and you say that she fled from the Muslims. When did this happen and where did she flee from?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this was during the fighting around Busovaca-Kacuni, and she lived around what was then a front line which is around Brestovsko, and actually, yes, she did flee, but her house was not destroyed, the houses were not destroyed, and there were people who remained there -- this is in the transcript from the film. There are some things that aren't -- of course, we have to cut -- and she went back the next day to check because they were worried about their house and their possessions, and some of the people remained to look after their house. She also mentions and a man -- and one of the men who were with her mention some of the Muslim neighbours who looked after their house and had told them, "You should leave because it is now dangerous for you here." But as I said, they did go back again, and as far as I know, they all moved back now. But there was fighting, and this was on the front line, the fighting between the HVO and the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Kacuni, that is to say, that you do know something about that village, do you? For example, do you know whether this was a Croat or a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know there were Muslims living there and there were Croats living there. I don't know how you would then define it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether there is a single Croat left living in Kacuni nowadays?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Whether they started to move back -- I know that there has been, between Fojnica and Kiseljak, there have been exchanges, so that both Muslims living in Croat houses in Fojnica and vice versa have been able to move back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: When you say that you don't know whether they came back -- I mean, the Croats into Kacuni -- is that to say that you know that they were expelled from there?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have no knowledge. It was when we were there the fighting was taking place. There was no way we could -- I have no knowledge of exactly what happened there. I know that both Muslim and Croat houses were destroyed and that there was intense fighting in -- well, I cannot remember right now the exact dates but while we were there at the end of January and February, but then that it calmed down. Because of that fighting, many people left this village near Kiseljak. Particularly the Muslims left. Then they came back again when it calmed down, because they thought that it had been resolved. That was why the village was quite full when it was attacked on the 18th of April by the HVO. It was full of Muslims because they'd come back. That's what I know. I drove through -- May we drove up with the U.N. escort and I did see houses. I saw houses belonging to both groups that had been destroyed, but I do not know anything about the military picture of what happened exactly and the different strength of the different forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were in Dusina, that you are familiar with this village, were you there at the time, at that time?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have visited it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: No one mentioned a thing to you? No one mentioned a massacre perhaps having taken place there?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Then, of course, I would have known. I would have remembered and known if that had been mentioned. I know that the village a very old village and that there are a couple of Croatian inhabited houses at the end of the village and the rest of Muslims houses. I do not know anything more about that village. I was not told -- and I believe that if the Croats in the area where I was had known about it at the time, they would have told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: So you talked to Croats, too, in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no. In the village where we did the film, sorry. I didn't talk to any people that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in the film we saw Bosnian soldiers at the front line and at home. We saw that they wore uniforms. We saw some who wore uniforms in part. Was this customary? Did some of them wear full uniforms, and some wore partial uniforms, and others yet wore civilian clothes only?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because they didn't have enough uniforms for everyone. Also, at the time they fought on the Serbian front line, as was mentioned in the film, toward Sarajevo, because most of these men worked in Sarajevo, and they were interested in trying to deblockade Sarajevo to be able to go back to work and also to help in trying to lift the siege of Sarajevo. So they had to go in shifts. They went every two weeks or so. It depended -- you know, they stayed two or three days and then they'd come back home. Yes. At that time they did not have uniforms, everybody, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: But we saw or, rather, I did not see a single person without an automatic rifle, at least not in this film. We saw that they had radio stations for communicating, and we saw mortar at one point. All of this was early 1993.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, of course, there was something called the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and these men were fighting in that army. I mean, that shouldn't be unknown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear, because we keep hearing that no such thing existed.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That I have not said. There was a government in Sarajevo leading a country --

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Did I say that? When?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you said it. I mean, I'm just saying that during this trial, we heard that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have any weapons, et cetera, et cetera. But tell me something else: Did civilians sometimes wear parts of camouflage clothes?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, certainly not. I mean, why -- I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Especially among the young people. Was it customary or perhaps because such clothes were available or I don't know what, but was it usual that people who did not belong to the military sometimes had jackets or other such items?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question because I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: All right. If you didn't see it, you didn't see it. When we saw one of these people whose house you were in go out for the village patrol, if I remember correctly, he wore a light blue jacket and his friend wore a dark jacket, and he had a light cap and the other one had a dark cap, and both of them had automatic weapons. Did I see this right?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did have weapons. That was not something that -- we mentioned that in the film. You probably know that in Bosnia, most men did have a weapon if they had been part of the reserve forces. That was nothing -- I honestly don't know what you're getting at because, yes, they did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: My question was -- well, I saw there, and I think that I saw this well, that they wore civilian clothes and that they were leaving their houses armed.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were not. They were guarding their homes. They were not out fighting as part of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Yes. All right. All right. But what I was interested in hearing is what you told me, that I saw this right, that they were wearing civilian clothes and that they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're talking about a group of two men. They went out in pairs and they went throughout these few houses. That's what they're talking about. They would come back and stay through the night and do this. This was common. As we talked about yesterday, the house was incredibly important for people. This is where not only their whole life savings they put into it, their life's work and savings, this is what they signified the unit, the household, which again was -- signified the whole group. It was where identity was formed. It was where they were socialised. It was where all important rituals took place. It was the unit for socialisation in the village. An attack on the house was seen as an attack on the very being of a person and his identity. It was much more than the destruction of a physical thing, and this is why the house was so important. That was destroying the family unit. It was seen as an attack on the group. This I've written about in my book, the significance of the house for identity. So it was very important to guard the house. This is what they did in areas it were they felt -- you know, where they saw there was a powerful army that may attack, and they could not mobilise the same thing. So they would protect -- they would protect their house, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: When you say that their houses were important to them, were they important to both ethnic groups? How important were they? Because I see in the film that -- well, yes, of course, houses are important because they invested a lot of work into their house and building their houses, et cetera. I also heard them say, "Forget about your house. The most important thing is to stay alive," which is only to be expected; right?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This was --

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: So was the situation the same with the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'll answer your first question. This was in the context of losing your children. It was in the context of rescuing your children and getting them out of harm's way. Now -- okay. The house -- in my analysis, the house is very important for both groups because, as I said, it's where you socialise your children and it's the unit of social action and all that, but I do believe that it also had a particular significance for the Muslims and I'll tell you why. This may be an academic argument, but anyway, it's the argument I have, is that identity for Muslims was not perceived in terms of blood. They would not talk about -- they would not say, "I'm Muslim by blood." Both Croats and Serbs would say that, meaning it's something you're born as. It's something that is almost genetic. Now, why so? Because the ethnic origin, of course, of the Muslims are the same as the Serbs and the Croats, or the Serbs or the Croats, we don't know which. Now, at one point in history, this indigenous population, they converted to Islam. So their identity was not initially an ethnic identity, it was an identity which was defined by your religion but then also morally -- through religion then morally and not by blood. This is often how they're -- they did talk about -- they did not refer to it by blood. So to me, what was important, what constituted then -- if you don't have this almost genetic or blood symbolism, then how do you define your identity? Well, through the environment and where you grow up, your moral environment. The house provided that moral environment which would embody your identity and so there is a slight difference. It's a very academic argument, but I can go into more detail if you're interested. That's why the house was very important, because it provided that moral environment where you acquired your identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: I did not understand why it would be different for Muslims, and Croats, and Serbs, if you wish. I mean, after all, they all have the same origin. I mean, you said so yourself, that the Muslims were Bogumils who converted to Islam because this was more convenient to them, but then never mind.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have not said what you just said. Don't rephrase me and say that I've said things that I haven't said. This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: I am just asking -- I mean, I said I did not understand why people of the same origin would all of a sudden feel -- some of them would feel that the house was more important to them and others would not feel that their houses were important. They'd been living together for centuries, so...

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, this is not what I was saying. I was saying that the house was important in rural communities. The houses are important for both groups, because it is the unit where your children are educated, socialised. It's where, you know, the rituals of the family unit evolve around a house. The house is the unit of interaction in the village. It's not -- you don't interact, which I write about, you don't interact as an individual, you interact as a member of a household. This is true for all groups. But then I said I'm making a very fine distinction which may -- it's my analysis of it, because I've been thinking about this a lot. Why this attack of the house? Why when storm-troopers or foot soldiers went into the house, why did they do particular things inside the houses? Why wasn't it just enough to shell the house? Why did they enter it? There must be something important here. I went into several of the houses in the village after they had been destroyed, and what I noticed was that they'd actually taken time to desecrate certain things that were central to Muslim identity. For instance, there was a dimija, which are these baggy trousers that Muslim women wear. They had been stuffed with hay and hung up. There were the fez of the old man which had actually been shit on. There was the beret, which is also a Muslim identity marker, which has been tossed about and dirtied in some way. I have heard this from other people and I wonder why. So there must be something about the house and these things that were symbolising Muslim identity. Why was it necessary to destroy that? That's what I'm trying -- you know, I'm trying to find out why.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, isn't it usual in a war that armies do bad things to the symbols of the other side? For example, I remember many cases when enemy flags were set fire to or something. In this case there weren't any flags, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: A flag --

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly. A flag is a different symbol though, because it --

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Even stronger, I should say.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- it symbolises the whole nation. This is something that you can, actually, to a certain extent distance yourself from. But these attacks are on the individual itself. It's their personal belonging. It's something they have worn. It's something they wear, each individual, to signify who they are, and a flag is something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did they perhaps enter houses and carry out their attacks in such a way perhaps because they did not have weapons with which they could destroy houses? We heard about military tactics here, about entering houses. For example, that one would use a tank to enter a house, not to go in through the door. Would that perhaps be a simpler reason that could be an explanation?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I doubt it, because these things were done after the military action. If you look at the damages that were done, in many cases it was done after, that could not possibly be done by hands. Some of these houses have obviously been shelled and burned. Say, the mosque in this particular village was destroyed after the military action . It was destroyed back in July, so after this had happened. So somebody had gone in there afterwards and done these things. Well, you can just use your eyes and look at the kind of destruction. I don't believe that that kind of destruction could have been outside, if you look at the house outside, could have been made just by bare hands. If you go inside, it's clear that somebody has been in there with their hands and done things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Very well. A few minutes ago you told me that I would have to know that men, as JNA reservists, had weapons, just as you explained to me yesterday that I did not necessarily have to understand things that are being said in the language that is my own. So you really believe that every JNA reservist had a weapon? So every man had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said men who were part of the reserve forces. Now, I don't know which men were given weapons and which weren't, but this was a gun that I know for sure that at least this particular man that you saw had back in 1980s. Now, I don't know how, you know, the JNA operated. That was not something I particularly looked into at the time. I do not know the rules for handing out weapons or why certain -- maybe if you were a member of the military police. I really don't know what the criterias were, but this is really beyond my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Well, this is mentioned in the case of Nurija, that he had a weapon for 15 years, a rifle, and also a general statement is made that he, like most men in the village, had a rifle because he was a JNA reservist, which is simply not true. I don't know whether I have to prove this particularly in Court that JNA reservists did not have weapons at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pasaric, could you ask questions and stick to our problem because some of your questions are really not relevant to the whole issue. The witness is an expert witness and she is a professor of anthropology, and she should testify on the general cultural background of the various communities. She is not a fact witness. Could you please move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you were translating your research, it is quite clear that in view of the subject of your research, you spent time in Muslim families. But tell me, when you filmed this TV programme, which is supposed to imply objectivity, there seems to be disproportionate time allocated to the other side, that is to say, to hear what happened to the other side; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: We went there, to this particular community, to film the effects of war on some families. Now, as you pointed out, when I did my research, for obvious reasons, back in the 1980s, I lived with a Muslim family. Now, in this sort of context, with a war going on and bringing in a film crew, it was very important that the people knew you well, and one was entirely practical, it was a practical solution to live there, and the crew then lived with a Croat family. I lived with this Muslim family. We did interview the Croats, as you say, in the film, but I do have to say that it was often difficult, and we were prevented from filming certain things. Now, in Croat houses, there were people in uniform, many in uniform, and I don't think they wanted us to film this, but I do not know. Again, this is something I can't answer. I can't answer why it was more difficult to get access to some of these things going on in the Croatian community. But, yes, we do because -- we do film the Muslims there. These other people who are -- it is a combination of two things: It's the people I knew the best, were these particular families, and also that this was the group that was under -- you know, most defensive in this situation, and we also see the results in April of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: If I notice correctly, in one part of your report, very brief mention is made of the fact that Croats were also victims of Muslim attacks, and you are telling me today, although this does not exist in the film, that that was not exactly the way it was, or, rather, that it was easier than what the film had portrayed, that people actually went back and, well ...

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I wanted to give you the context because you were asking me that -- that came out in a completely different context about -- you talked about Kacuni and so on. No, we let the people talk. I mean, just as we did with the Croats, we did with the Bosniaks. We let them talk and give their version of it. We don't come in and say, "But, listen, you know, they went back the other day," or "Listen, it was not quite ..." But this is the people's perception of what was going on and it's about their lives and how they deal with the war. Now, part of the interview says that. It does tell you -- I was telling you that in the context of a different question, that these people went back to their house, that they had not -- they were not, as such, ethnically cleansed from that village. They had not been all expelled and all their houses burned down and destroyed. That was my point. But I am not saying that this -- you know, that Croats were not victims. That's not what I'm saying. Of course, there were Croat victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Tell me, may I ask you the following: In the forward to your book, page xx in Roman numerals, you mention that two readers from the Princeton University Press helped you a lot. You have not identified them. Would that be -- can we know what they did and who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What is the relevance? What is the relevance of your question? These are readers. In all --

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: They are anonymous. They are anonymous. Readers are anonymous for press. I do not know who they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. Any serious publishing company, Oxford University Press, Princeton University Press and so on, normally resort to two readers to check on the quality of the scholarly contribution. We authors, we don't -- well, the authors don't know the name of the readers. Besides, even if Professor Bringa knew the name of those two readers, what is the relevance of your question, if I may ask you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: I simply wished to see because -- well, I'm afraid -- well, I'm afraid that these entire statements in the film are a bit one-sided, I'm afraid, and these were important influences that are being mentioned, so I wanted to ascertain who these people were. And, of course, if Mrs. Bringa doesn't know the identity of these persons, well, then, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: You said that you are familiar with the subject of this trial. Also, in the forward to your book, you mention, as a scholar, that in Bosnia, there were many different ways in which persons from different communities lived together and that their ways differed from one town to another, from one family to another, from one village to another. Tell me, if you are familiar with the subject of this trial, at least in general terms, and since a lot has been written about the subject of this trial, do you know of any differences that existed between the village that you called Dolina and the situation in Ahmici or the area of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know that area. I cannot say anything about it because I don't know that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Sorry. You said that you knew about this trial, so I had assumed that you knew a bit, perhaps about these differences that might exist.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you know, the only differences I may think of is maybe in the composition. Now, I don't know the statistics of Ahmici, I don't know how many were Muslims and how many were Croats and possibly -- where it was situated, I don't know anything about the history of the village, I don't know anything about the particular relationship between particular neighbours in the village, so I really can't be helpful. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: It is hard for me to find the exact point in time, but I think this was during your first visit. It seems that at that time already, the Croats were digging themselves in above the village and creating these firing positions.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was towards, I think, the end of our stay, so it must have been in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Or in early February?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I left the 13th. I really can't recall when that must have taken place but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Muslims in Dolina undertook some military operations as early as 1992, that is, against the Croats, or even set up some checkpoints, in the late fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Can you specify what you mean by "military action"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: For the most part, you say that things were quiet in Dolina. Do you know whether there were such actions, such as setting up of checkpoints by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were no Bosnian army checkpoints where we were at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: How about the relations between the Muslims and the Croats? If I understood you correctly, they became more tense and broke off during that first period; right? That is, in January-February, during your first visit.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is what is described in the film, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: In other words, they no longer had contact among themselves.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge and not the people that we were describing in the film. I don't know about every single individual. There may have been people who still had contact, but I would not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- Dolina was part of the Kiseljak municipality, but does Kiseljak border directly on Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Does it have a direct link --

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... geographically. No. As far as I remember, you have to cross a mountain, like you often have to do in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: The question is, was the communication between Kiseljak and Herzegovina ever severed? Was Kiseljak ever surrounded by the Bosniak forces?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: You know, I did not travel in that region throughout the whole war. When we were there, there was access from Herzegovina, yes. There were roads that were opened and kept open. I could not answer your question because I do not know about military formations throughout those years of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: But you could pass through even the second time when you came.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: With the convoys -- the road was kept open by the U.N. and there were convoys. You had to go by convoy on that main road. I don't know about other roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: In the film, it is said that Muslims could not gather in larger groups than three. Was that also the case when you came around in January-February?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was in January-February. I think we're ... Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: So the gathering of Muslims in Dolina was banned in January-February.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is described in the film. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: I also found it interesting that you mention, regarding the celebration of Bajram, some Croats allegedly said that if anybody wanted to celebrate Bajram, that they should go to Visoko; is that what you heard them say?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: What I was talking about was this gradual redefinition of the Kiseljak area as purely Croatian where people of non-Croatian background felt that they had no place or did not belong, and there were many things that came together that made people feel that this was not their place anymore. One of the episodes was this one, where someone who worked at a kindergarten where they had introduced the celebration of Christmas for the children, asked, "What shall we do then when Orthodox Christmas comes up and when Bajram comes up? How should we organise these celebrations?" And the answer she got from her superior at the kindergarten was that those who want to celebrate Bajram should go to Visoko, which was then seen as a Muslim-controlled area or Muslim place, whatever that might mean; and those who want to celebrate Orthodox Christmas should go, I cannot now quite remember, but it was an area which was then considered Serbian. This was just an example to show how gradually a place which had -- a space which had earlier been shared by people of different ethnic backgrounds was then gradually being redefined as purely Croatian, purely one thing or the other, purely Croatian, whereas the others did not have a place where -- their traditions, their culture had no place. If they wanted to continue being Muslim or Serb, whatever that was not Croatian, they should go somewhere else. This is it. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: My question was only: When did this happen, approximately?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, approximately -- I believe it must have been maybe '92. I couldn't tell you. '91, '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: I found it interesting that you mention in your book that there were only three mixed marriages in Dolina, and those were marriages between a Muslim and a Serbian woman, and in the village itself, the population mix really consisted of the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: I know that we belabour this point with folk groups, but this young Muslim woman, Suhreta, in the tape, mentions that in the folk group, it was not important who you were. It was not important who you "were"; she speaks in past tense. Does that mean that this folk group that she is referring to no longer existed at the time when she was talking about it?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if it did in some form or another, she would not probably maybe be able to go there. I believe it did not, no. It had stopped. She did not attend it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: The book also mentions, and this is in the context of mixed marriages but I would like to know whether this was generally the case, that in the towns, especially among the educated class, the socioeconomic aspects were more important than the ethnic ones; in other words, what I'm interested in is whether the attitudes shifted in that direction the more urbanised an environment was?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: The more urbanised or the more educated, let's say, the sub-groups were.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean the less they would oppose mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not so interested in mixed marriages in this context but whether the people who were more urbanised or who lived closer to towns and cities and who were better educated, that they were less inclined to view everything through an ethnic filter, so to speak. Was that the tendency?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was often true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Dolina was the last village in the Kiseljak municipality which was subjected to an attack; in other words, the war had raged around them and they had been spared.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe there were some villages further south of this village, closer to Sarajevo, that then were then also subject to attacks, they were a bit later, but it was one of the last, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: You mentioned something that I also found interesting yesterday regarding the architecture. At a later stage, they shared the same type, but the Croat houses were different in one other way. I never thought about it because that had disappeared in the cities. But did they have a blessing written in chalk on them? You mentioned crosses.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- yes. I do not -- I had not observed that in that particular village. I mean, the cross, yes, yes, but not written --

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: So what type of cross was it?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, what type of cross? I mean, the Catholic, Christian -- or where was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Where was it, yes.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know the technical term for that place of the house, but if you have a house like this (indicating), okay, which this is the long side, the long side here, this is the short side, so it was up underneath where the roof meets. Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pasaric, may I ask you to be so kind as to wind up?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I am almost finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Did all or most of the Croat houses have this?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The houses in the old part of the town, all the houses that were built in an old architectural form that distinguishes themselves from the Muslim ones, they had it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: In the village, did the newly-built houses also have it?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not observe it in this village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: On page 53 of the transcript, in reference to the film, Mrs. Slavka, after the attack, when you asked her, allegedly told you that the soldiers came early in the morning and that they were going to attack another village, and only later did they warn her that they were going to attack this village which then actually took place. It would seem that the army did not have confidence in the villagers, in other words, that they did not reveal to them their intentions.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not able to answer that question. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: It was only said that --

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is what she says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Also, when it is said that brothers of Mrs. Sahida were killed and that this was done by next-door neighbours, do you know whether the identity of the perpetrators was revealed to her or to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: She says she knows the identity of the killers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, that the next-door neighbours did so. But since you knew these people, did she tell you who these people were or identify them in any other way?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Neither did I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you were not interested in those names, but do you know whether she informed other people of the identity of those people or whether she just left it at, they were the next-door neighbours?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Just one additional question which goes to your expertise rather than to what you talked about. If you were to be told that in Vitez there was a folk group in existence and that after the divisions which subsequently took place, that a Muslim and a Croatian group were established but that some Croats still maintained the original group and that Bajram and Easter were celebrated alongside each other; would that mean something to you, that context? The question is: Was there a significant difference between Dolina and Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't really quite understand what you're getting at. You're telling me something which is an interesting piece of ethnography, but I don't know anything more about the context of it. So I reserve myself to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: If you take what I just said, if they were true would that represent a significant difference between Dolina and Ahmici, that is, the fact that in Ahmici-Vitez, the Muslim Bajram was celebrated by Croats and Muslims, and that some Croats maintained a full group which united both despite the fact that separate folk groups had been established around? Would that, in other words, represent a significant difference at the time when whatever you experienced in Dolina was already taking place?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The folk group that these women are referring to is in Kiseljak. Now, I was not, unfortunately, particularly interested in dance and music. I focused on other things. I think there was an anthropologist who dealt with that. So I don't know what was the state of that folk group. Obviously, I should have asked when I was there, but there were lots of other things going on then. So I don't know whether they may have had something similar. So I can't tell you anything about the difference because I don't know the state of that folk group in Kiseljak. I don't know whether they also were celebrating Bajram and Easter in the same way.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, which month are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Bajram in 1993 was in March.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Obviously they were not because there were no Muslims left to celebrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: But I assume then in March 1993 --

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. I cannot -- I mean, I cannot answer your question where I don't have the ethnographic information, not to context what was going on. I mean, this is very bad scholarship if I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PASARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have any questions. Yes, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, a single question. I needed to establish a certain fact. It has not been asked and I just need to specify something.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Professor, my name is Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac, and I really need just to ask you one question in regarding facts in relation to the tape you made. I know you made a portion of it in January and February '93 and then subsequently another one in April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you recollect when were the first portions of the film taped, the ones that are referred to in the videotape as part 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The whole film, except when we say, "Eight weeks after." I don't know if that is on your tape, that there is break and then it says, "Eight weeks after." That whole first part was filmed in January and February when we were there the first time for three weeks. Then there's a break. I think it says -- it should say "Eight weeks later," which starts with when I come out of the car and meet the people in front of the house. That was taken in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. I had assumed that it was taped earlier. Thank you for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. So we don't have any questions. Professor Bringa, thank you so much for coming to The Hague to give evidence in Court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I suggest we adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Our witness is Mr. Majstorovic. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to apologise for interrupting you, but it seems to me I owe you an answer in relation to Slavko Marin's testimony. I wish to state now that the Defence has given up on this witness altogether, and I wish to confirm this officially now to my colleague the Prosecutor as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you whether this is because Mr. Slavko Marin is not prepared to come over to The Hague or because it is part of your policy, I mean, your legal strategy not it call him, if I may ask you? Only because the Prosecutor raised this matter. If you want to refrain from answering my question, of course you are entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I shall answer and I shall be quite brief. It is a question of the second matter that you mentioned. Our assessment was that things were clear enough as they stand, and we believe that in this way we are contributing to shortening the proceedings as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Counsel Pavkovic. No comments from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Not for the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much, so we can move on. Mr. Majstorovic, could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself to the Court? Tell us where you live, when you were born, and what you do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My name is Dragan Majstorovic. I was born on the 21st of March, 1968 in Zenica. At present I live in the municipality of Vitez, Hrvatskih Branitelja B/43. Since 1994 I have worked as an official in the defence department of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what your education has been?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: I have completed a post-secondary economic school for commerce.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you work in the defence department of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us your exact job description?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, I took up a job as an expert officer for structures outside the arms forces, and from 1995 I have been a higher senior officer for mobilisation and manning the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you explain briefly, as briefly as possible, how mobilisation is carried out regularly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Regularly. Well, in order to carry out mobilisation, certain preliminary action has been taken, that is to say, that every military unit has to have its mobilisation documents. In this case, these are mobilisation call-up papers. This is the MOB 11 form, as it is known, and it is sent by way of messenger in order to call up a conscript for military exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is such mobilisation customary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: This is the normal way to carry out mobilisation. In addition to that there is a public call to mobilisation by way of the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is mobilisation, in certain extraordinary circumstances, carried out in the same way as you described it just now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Naturally mobilisation has to be carried out in this way in order to trace the documents that are being sent, that is to say, the call-up papers, so that if call-up papers are not responded to, then on the basis of these mail documents, criminal proceedings can be instituted against the person in question, that is to say, the military conscript who does not respond to call-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In order to carry out mobilisation in any circumstances, even in an extraordinary situation, is it necessary for some time to take place? Is it possible to mobilise 1.000 men during the course of one day, for example?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: As the situation stands right now, it could be carried out but in the times of war it was impossible. Any military unit has a certain time period involved for carrying out full mobilisation. At present, right now, this required time is 24 hours, but in '93 and '94 this was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why was it impossible at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: For a simple reason. At that time, military formations did not have a well-elaborated mobilisation system. Also, the system of messengers, that is to say, of delivering call-up papers had not been elaborated, and also because of combat action that was taking place throughout the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there a list of reservists that existed at that time as well that could have been accurate, that could have included all the particulars, that is say, addresses and the current addresses of a person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, did the defence department, which was supposed to carry out mobilisation at that time also; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, did it have proper lists of reservists with all the particulars of the persons involved and all their current addresses, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, what is the difference between the reserve forces and the active forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: The reserve forces are reserve forces as we used to call them in the previous system. During war and cases of immediate threat of war, there is no difference. Naturally, when there is no war there is a major difference. The reserve force is demobilised. These people normally go to work, while the active force is mobilised all the time. They are in uniform non-stop and they are paid appropriately for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that during the war there is no difference between the reserve force and the active force, and is there a difference between the reserve force and the active force during the danger of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: During the war there was no difference for a simple reason, because everyone had the same task and they were altogether at the front lines, the defence lines, whereas after the war they had jobs. I hope you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who actually makes up the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: The reserve force consists of all military-aged men, that is to say, from the age of 17 to 60, whereas in cases of war and immediate threat of war, the age limit to 65 for members of the civilian defence and also people who have work duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How important is the oath that is taken by soldiers, that is to say, by reservists or military conscripts or ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: An oath is taken only once in the lifetime of a military conscript, that is to say, when the oath is taken for the army of that State. However, since the former Yugoslavia had fallen apart into several statelets, the establishment of all new formations in the territory of the former Yugoslavia meant that all units had to take this oath. This was a formality, that is to say, that they would swear that they would be proper soldiers of that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Does this oath have any other significance except for it being a ceremonial occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: No. It's just a ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can a person become a soldiers in a unit without taking an oath?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: One more thing related to the status of the reserve force. You said that during the war the active force and the reserve force have the same status. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: During the war and during an immediate threat of war, the reserve force are actually civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And is there any difference at that stage between a reservist and a military conscript, terminologically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: No. Everybody is a member of the reserve force and a military conscript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say that all military-aged men and military conscripts are the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the additional job that you took on in 1996?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: In 1996, when the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted on additional salaries for members of the HVO, I was head of the working group for calculating additional salaries for members of the HVO for the time they spent in the military forces during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of making these lists?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of making these lists was to make it possible for all participants in the war to be paid, at least retroactively, for the time they spent in units of the MUP, the army units, that is to say, then the Ministry of Interior units and to members of units who had work duty, and to all other units that in some way took part in carrying out defence tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the basis of which rule was this obligation of the state established?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: All three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina sooner or later worked on the elaboration of these lists for additional pay. I do not know on the basis of what parliament had voted on this law concerning additional pay, but I also know that the military component of the HVO was not the first one to start this. This took place later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say that the other two peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina also did the same kind of mathematics and also passed regulations allowing this additional pay to be given?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the basis of which particular regulations? Would you tell us exactly on the basis of which law was this obligation established in view of the Croat component?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: In the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 16/96, from the 25th of April, 1996. That is when this law on additional salaries was voted on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: For the sake of precision, and since this particular information is very important for us in order to look into certain lists, could you tell us precisely which categories of persons were included in these calculations, that is to say, which categories of persons were recognised the right to have this additional salary paid out to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: The right to additional pay was enjoyed by all members of the active and reserve forces of the HVO; officials and members of the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say, the police; members of the civilian defence who, during that period of time, were under the competencies of the Ministry of the Interior; also all participants war, that is to say, invalids from 20 to 100 per cent invalidity. Then also all recorded military conscripts who were missing, all who took part in the war for their homeland, and all other participants who took part in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What is this referred to? Is this stated in the law itself or were there separate instructions that were issued?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Later, after the law on additional pay was promulgated, then all the defence departments received instructions as to how these additional salaries would be calculated, that is to say, how these additional salaries would be calculated where the protagonists of this activity were specified and also the way in which this could be checked and calculated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The lists that were made on that occasion were sent to the defence department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This was done in the territory of your municipality too; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which list of which unit was sent to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: All units that had military conscripts in the territory of the municipality of Vitez were duty-bound to send to their own defence department a list of all persons who were engaged during a certain period of time. This was supposed to be sent to the defence department, except for military post code 1779 Vitez. They, during the war, were called the Vitez Brigade, and from 1994 they were called the 92nd Home Guard Regiment. Then a list was obtained. Then from military post code 1711, that is the Home Guard Battalion, independent battalion of Zenica. During the war, it was called the Zenica Brigade. The remaining smaller units that were in the territory of the municipality of Vitez, such as the military police, the mixed artillery division, the anti-aircraft defence, the signals company, and other officers who were employed in the military district of Vitez and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting. That is to say, that these units that you mentioned, the MUP, the military police, the PZO, that is to say, the anti-aircraft defence, members of headquarters, these were actually persons who were on a separate list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The list was called "Other Units."

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, was another list made?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There is a list of work duty units, that is to say, this was supplied by companies that had work duty during the war. Then there was a list that said HDZ, and there was a later -- there was a later list that was also marked HDZ, but the list of HDZ that I have mentioned is the list of village guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to show the witness Prosecutor's Exhibit P353.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Majstorovic, this is the list. This is a list that was issued by your office too, and this is one of the lists that was submitted to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What is this list out of the ones that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: That is the list of the military post code 1711, and that is the Vitez Brigade, and then later it turned into the Home Guard Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The forms which are the contents of this list, who filled them out: you or the unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: The unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The markings which are marked as "Status," could you look at them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was entering those?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: These markings had to be entered in these forms. It is called PP1. They had to stick to those markings, so in the instructions, "PP" means "Pukovnija" and "Reserve."

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So that "P" is "Precuva" --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJSTOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.
